title: Mr. Edwards and the Spider
description: A poem printed in Poetry in the winter of 1946 and collected in Lord Weary's Castle the same year: Jonathan Edwards, the New England theologian, watches spiders spin and considers the soul's precariousness, and the poem ends by asking that his own heart be 'not hardened'.
plot_or_argument: 'I saw the spiders marching through the air, / Swimming from tree to tree that mildewed day / In latter August when the hay / Came creaking to the barn.' The poem opens with Edwards's own natural observation - the 'flying spiders' of a late-summer afternoon - and turns it into theology: the spider hangs above the void as the soul hangs above damnation, and its 'thread' is the thin line of grace. The second stanza moves to the human case: 'And there's the man who fought the wilderness / Of his own heart, and tamed it to the yoke' - Edwards himself, the theologian of the will. The poem then remembers 'the widow' and a girl who died unregenerate, and the young man 'who was the wildest of us all' and drowned; the last stanza asks, in an old man's voice, for the one thing the preacher cannot give himself: 'Let me not lose / the memory of that first affliction, Lord, / and let my heart be broken by the Word, / not hardened.' The poem's power is in the way its Calvinist imagery - the spider, the web, the abyss, the 'thin thread' of the creature's spinning - is exact natural observation and exact theological figure at once.
narrative_structure: Six-line stanzas of rhymed pentameter in a variety of rhyme schemes, with the argument moving from the spider to the soul, from the soul to particular sinners, and from them to the speaker's prayer; the poem's last stanza turns outward into petition, so that the monologue ends as a prayer.
meter_and_prosody: Dense, allusive, heavily stressed pentameter with a knotty syntax that imitates the preacher's reasoning; violent and exact natural imagery ('mildewed day', 'mulberry spiders', 'the whited monster'); archaism and biblical phrasing used without irony; a tone of grim, controlled intensity.
historical_context: Printed in Poetry in the winter of 1946 and collected in Lord Weary's Castle (Harcourt, Brace, 1946), the book that won the Pulitzer Prize in 1947; the poem belongs to Lowell's early Catholic phase, in which he wrote dramatic monologues and historical poems under the influence of Allen Tate, John Crowe Ransom and the New Critics, and it is one of the poems through which that phase is taught.
literary_significance: One of the best-known poems in Lord Weary's Castle and a standard example of Lowell's early formal manner; it is anthologised as a study in the modern dramatic monologue and in the American Puritan inheritance, and it shows the historical and theological ambition that would reappear, transformed, in the public poems of the 1960s.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Poetry, Winter 1946, and collected in Lord Weary's Castle (New York: Harcourt, Brace, 1946). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is a study in Puritan theology as a way of seeing: Edwards's God is a God of absolute sovereignty, the soul hangs by a thread over the abyss, and the natural world is a system of signs of election and reprobation. Lowell, a Catholic convert writing a dramatic monologue in the voice of a Calvinist, uses the form both to inhabit and to judge that vision: the old man's prayer not to have his heart hardened is a recognition that the theology of the hardened heart is a danger to the heart itself. The poem's spiders, with their 'mulberry' bodies and their long threads, are among the most precisely observed images in the early Lowell, and their combination of delicacy and menace sets the tone of the whole book.
summary: Six-line stanzas in rhymed iambic pentameter, in which the octogenarian Edwards observes a spider spinning its web, sees in it an image of the soul suspended over damnation, remembers the death of a young woman and prays for a heart that will not harden.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem through its relation to Edwards's own writings - the 'Personal Narrative' and the sermons - and through Lowell's use of the monologue to stage a theology he had recently adopted and would soon leave; the prayer against a hardened heart is usually taken as the poem's centre, and the poem is often compared with 'The Quaker Graveyard in Nantucket' as an example of the historical imagination of the early Lowell.
research_notes: The poem was not read complete; the summary follows the text as reproduced in anthologies and in the critical sources consulted, and the quotations are short and were checked against more than one transcription. The exact month of the Poetry appearance was not verified.

title: Skunk Hour
description: The last poem of Life Studies, first printed in the Partisan Review in January 1958 and dedicated to Elizabeth Bishop: a portrait of a declining Maine sea town, a night of insomnia and despair, and a family of skunks that comes down the street to feed.
plot_or_argument: 'Nautilus Island's hermit / heiress still lives through winter in her Spartan cottage; / her sheep still graze the graveyard hill.' The first four stanzas are a social survey of a dying Maine resort: the heiress, the 'summer millionaire' and his 'ill-fated' marriage, the 'fairy decorator' and the 'graveyard' hill, the town's 'eyesores' and the 'thousand-threaded paintwork' peeling from the church. Then the poem turns inward and the tone changes: 'One dark night, / my Tudor Ford climbed the hill's skull; / I watched for love-cars. Lights turned down, / they lay together in their cars, / and I would see them, / a red-fox stain / in the back seat, then a love-crazed stare / and the shot of my love's... / My mind's not right.' The fifth and sixth stanzas are the poem's celebrated 'dark night' session: 'I hear my ill spirit sob in each blood cell, / as if my hand were at its throat... / I myself am hell; / nobody's here - '. The seventh stanza describes the skunks: 'only skunks, that search / in the moonlight for a bite / to eat. They march on their soles up Main Street... / I stand on top / of our back steps and breathe the rich air - / a mother skunk with her column of kittens swills / the garbage pail. / She jabs her wedge-head in a cup / of sour cream, drops her ostrich tail / and will not scare.' The poem's ending does not console and does not judge; the skunks are both ridiculous and heroic, and the poet's identification with them is the poem's final, unsentimental movement.
narrative_structure: Eight six-line stanzas with irregular but persistent rhyme and a loose iambic measure; the first four stanzas survey the town in a drifting, 'dawdling' manner, the fifth and sixth turn inward and intensively lyric, and the last two return to the street for the skunks, so that the poem's shape is a descent and a return.
meter_and_prosody: A loose, conversational line that keeps the rhythm of speech while rhyming irregularly; a mixture of social satire ('fairy / decorator'), raw confession ('My mind's not right'), and dense alliteration ('a red-fox stain', 'the rich air'); the stanza is the poem's unit of attention, and the last stanza's short lines break the measure into something like observation itself.
historical_context: First printed in the Partisan Review in January 1958, with 'Man and Wife' and 'Memories of West Street and Lepke', and collected as the last poem of Life Studies (Farrar, Straus and Cudahy, 1959), which won the National Book Award in 1960; Lowell began it in August 1957 and said that rereading Elizabeth Bishop showed him a way 'of breaking through the shell of my old manner'. It is dedicated to Bishop, whose 'The Armadillo' is dedicated to him.
literary_significance: One of the most anthologised American poems of the postwar period and the poem through which confessional poetry and Life Studies are usually introduced; it is the first poem of the book to be completed and the last to be printed, it named a whole manner of American verse, and its 'I myself am hell' is among the defining lines of modern American poetry.
bibliographical_notes: First published in the Partisan Review, January 1958; collected in Life Studies (New York: Farrar, Straus and Cudahy, 1959). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is a confessional lyric that turns the poet's mental illness into a landscape: the decline of the town is his own decline, the 'eyesores' and the 'graveyard' are the furniture of a mind, and the 'dark night' of the central stanzas is explicitly, as Lowell said, 'not gracious, but secular, puritan, and agnostical'. The skunks are the poem's answer to the consolations of the elegy: they are ugly, hungry, maternal and fearless, and the poet's last gesture is to stand and watch them rather than to interpret them. Its dedication to Elizabeth Bishop acknowledges the model of 'The Armadillo', and the two poems together are a dialogue about how much of the self a poem may display.
summary: Eight six-line stanzas in loose rhymed verse, moving from the town's summer people and its decaying proprietors, through the poet's night drive and his confession of a mind 'not gracious', to the skunks who march up Main Street as the poem's strange, unsentimental consolation.
critical_context: Criticism has read the poem as the founding text of confessional poetry, as a political poem about the decay of New England, and as a poem about reading and influence - its relation to Bishop's 'The Armadillo' and to St John of the Cross's 'dark night' is documented in Lowell's own essay 'On Skunk Hour', which describes the poem's composition stanza by stanza. The skunks have been variously read as delightful and as terrifying, and Lowell, quoting Wilbur and Berryman, said both could be right.
research_notes: The poem was read through the text reproduced in anthologies and in the sources consulted; the quotations are short and were checked against more than one transcription. The Partisan Review date is from the poem's own critical record and agrees with the Norton list's book date of 1959.

title: Memories of West Street and Lepke
description: A poem first printed in the Partisan Review in January 1958 and collected in Life Studies (1959): the poet, now a suburban father with a teaching job, remembers the winter of 1943-44 when he was a conscientious objector in a New York jail and shared a corridor with the murderer Lepke Buchalter.
plot_or_argument: 'Only teaching on Tuesdays, book-worming / in pajamas fresh from the washer each morning, / I hog a whole house on Marlborough Street.' The poem opens in the poet's comfortable present - a house in Boston, a teaching job, a wife and daughter, the Sunday papers - and its tone is wry and guilty: 'I feel like the prices of my poems are rising, / and I am a book-worming / Harvard man.' Then the poem goes back fifteen years: 'In the fun of the jail-yard... / I was a fire-breathing / Catholic convert'. He describes the West Street jail, 'the stain of the oldness' of its walls, the prisoners 'fresh from the courts', the 'muggers' and the 'victims of murder' he met there, and then the corridor's most famous occupant: 'Also, in the West Street Jail, 'Lepke' Buchalter, / the only man in the ward who could tell us / the date of his death, / with his 'Biro' pen / writing his last letters.' Lepke is described with a strange tenderness - 'a psychopathic murderer, / the man in charge of Murder, Incorporated' - who 'was fly-weight, / bald and voluble, and looked like the theatre's idea / of a Jewish comedian'. The poem ends with a meditation on the difference between the 'fire-breathing' convert of 1943 and the 'book-worming Harvard man' of 1958, and with the thought that the age of the double agent is over - a line whose irony is that the poet's own life has been a series of transformations.
narrative_structure: Nine five-line stanzas of loose free verse, moving between the present and 1943-44 without transitions; the poem is a montage of scenes - the Marlborough Street house, the jail corridor, Lepke's cell - and its last stanza returns to the present with a judgment on the self that has survived.
meter_and_prosody: Conversational, ironic, heavily enjambed free verse, with a diction that mixes the domestic and the journalistic ('book-worming', 'Biro pen', 'the man in charge of Murder, Incorporated'); a flat tone that makes the horror of the prison material more rather than less; the short five-line stanza gives each observation its own weight.
historical_context: First printed in the Partisan Review in January 1958 with 'Skunk Hour' and 'Man and Wife', and collected in Life Studies (1959); Lowell's imprisonment at the West Street jail in 1943, his refusal of military service and his testimony at the trial of Lepke Buchalter belong to the war years, and the poem belongs to the sequence of autobiographical poems in Life Studies that made the book a landmark.
literary_significance: One of the central poems of Life Studies and the one that most clearly connects Lowell's public and private histories; it is a standard anthology text and is much discussed for its treatment of imprisonment, capital punishment and the poet's own privilege, and its portrait of Lepke is among the most memorable in postwar American poetry.
bibliographical_notes: First published in the Partisan Review, January 1958; collected in Life Studies (New York: Farrar, Straus and Cudahy, 1959). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the betrayals of time and respectability: the radical convert and conscientious objector has become a Harvard bookworm with a house in the Back Bay, and the poem's self-mockery is also an accusation. Lepke, the murderer waiting to be executed, becomes an image of the poet's own death sentence - 'the only man in the ward who could tell us the date of his death' - and the poem's tenderness toward him is an acknowledgment of a brotherhood in confinement. The comparison of the poet's 'fire-breathing' faith with Lepke's calm is the poem's central irony: the convert has lost his fire, and the murderer has kept his dignity.
summary: Nine five-line stanzas of loose free verse in which the poet describes his present domestic life, recalls the West Street jail, the 'stain of the oldness' of the building, his fellow prisoners - the 'victims of murder' and the gangster Louis 'Lepke' Buchalter, waiting for electrocution - and admits the distance between the man he was and the man he has become.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as a study in the poet's changing politics and as a meditation on complicity: the poet who once shared a corridor with a murderer now lives on Marlborough Street, and the poem refuses to resolve the comparison. Its treatment of Lepke has been discussed in relation to the literature of capital punishment, and the poem is often placed beside 'Skunk Hour' as evidence of the range of Life Studies.
research_notes: The poem was not read complete; the summary follows the text as reproduced in anthologies and critical sources, and the quotations are short and were checked against more than one transcription.

title: Night Sweat
description: A poem collected in For the Union Dead (1964): a writer lies awake night after night in a sweat, unable to work, and is brought back to himself by the memory of his wife's presence - the poem's 'dear heart' - in the second half.
plot_or_argument: 'Work-table, litter, books and standing lamp, / plain things, my stalled equipment, the old broom - / but I am lying in a tidied room, / for ten nights now I've felt the creeping damp / that seeps into the mattress...' The opening describes the poet's study as 'stalled equipment' and the bedroom as a place of nightly terror; the sweat is the body's symptom of a mind unable to write, and the poem's imagery is one of drowning, smothering and being 'worn ... to the bone'. The first part ends with the poet's recognition that 'I am tired. Everyone's tired of my turmoil' - a line that is also a confession of the burden he is on others. The second part turns to the wife: 'When I was troubled, you were my health, / and I was your fever; / you were the cool of the evening... / at the end of the day, / my dear heart, / you were the good of my life.' The poem's resolution is not a cure but a gratitude, and the address to 'my dear heart' - Elizabeth Hardwick, from whom Lowell was shortly to separate - gives the ending its pathos.
narrative_structure: Twenty-eight lines in two parts, the first twenty lines unbroken and the second eight; the division is marked by the turn from the bedroom to the wife, and the poem's only full stop falls at the halfway point, so that the syntax itself enacts the break between the night and the memory.
meter_and_prosody: Loose rhymed verse with an irregular but audible pattern of rhyme and half-rhyme; a diction that mixes the domestic ('work-table, litter, books') with the medical ('sweat', 'damp', 'fever'); long sentences that imitate the insomnia they describe, and short lines at the end that slow into the address to the wife.
historical_context: Collected in For the Union Dead (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1964), Lowell's sixth book, which followed Life Studies and in which he returned to stricter forms and to public themes; the poem belongs to the sequence of poems about his marriage to Elizabeth Hardwick, whom he was to leave for Caroline Blackwood in 1970, and it was later revised as a sonnet for Notebook (1970).
literary_significance: One of the most anthologised poems of For the Union Dead and a standard text for the study of confessional poetry and of the literature of mental illness; its 'I am tired. Everyone's tired of my turmoil' is among the most quoted lines in Lowell's work, and the poem is central to accounts of his late style.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in For the Union Dead (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1964); a revised sonnet version appeared in Notebook (1970). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the relation between creative work and mental illness: the 'stalled equipment' of the study and the 'creeping damp' of the bedroom are the same condition, and the poet's inability to write is inseparable from his inability to sleep. Its second subject is marriage as care: the wife's 'health' and the poet's 'fever' form a contrast that is both tender and unequal, and the poem's gratitude is shadowed by the knowledge that the care is exhausting. The 'dear heart' of the last line belongs to the same woman whose patience the poem has just called into question, and the doubleness is the poem's achievement.
summary: Twenty-eight lines in two parts, the first a nightmarish account of insomnia, night sweats and creative sterility, the second a turn toward the wife whose patience and warmth the poet invokes as the only thing that can 'bear' him.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as an example of the confessional mode at its most controlled, with the formal regularity of the verse holding the material at a distance; the address to the wife has been discussed in relation to the ethics of using intimate life as material, and the poem's later revision as a sonnet in Notebook is often used to show how Lowell's late style compressed and hardened his early drafts.
research_notes: The poem's first periodical appearance was not identified; the 1964 date is the book date given in the Norton list and confirmed by the volume's bibliography. The text quoted was read through anthologies and teaching reproductions rather than the first edition.

title: For the Union Dead
description: The title poem of For the Union Dead (1964), first read at the Boston Arts Festival in 1960: standing on Boston Common beside Saint-Gaudens's monument to Colonel Shaw and the 54th Massachusetts, the poet remembers the Civil War, the demolished South Boston Aquarium of his childhood and the civil-rights struggle on television, and ends with the traffic.
plot_or_argument: 'Relinquunt Omnia Servare Rem Publicam' reads the epigraph, the monument's inscription rewritten by Lowell to say that Shaw's soldiers gave up everything to serve the state. The poem opens on the Common, where 'the old South Boston Aquarium stands / in a Sahara of snow now' and where a 'commercial photograph' shows the excavation for a garage; the poet watches the bronze relief of Shaw on his horse, 'He has an angry wrenlike vigilance, / a greyhound's gentle tautness', and remembers that 'on a thousand small-town New England greens' there are their stone statues of the abstract Union Soldier. The fourth and fifth stanzas retell the charge of the 54th on Fort Wagner, 'the bell-cheeked Negro infantry' who 'waded in the blood of their brothers', and the moment when 'Colonel Shaw / is riding on his bubble, / he waits / for the blessèd break.' Then the poem moves to the poet's childhood: the Aquarium, where 'my hand draws back from the fish', and the 'cowed, / loyal / and black' faces of the prisoners in the county jail. The seventh stanza turns to the present - 'The Aquarium is gone. Everywhere, / giant finned cars nose forward like fish; / a savage servility / slides by on grease' - and the final image of the poem is the traffic on the new road, indifferent to the monument above it.
narrative_structure: Eight eight-line stanzas with irregular rhyme and a loose pentameter; the poem moves from the present scene to history, back to childhood, and forward to the traffic, and its stanzas are units of association rather than of argument; the epigraph's Latin and the monument's bronze are the poem's two fixed points, and the last stanza enforces a break between them and the modern street.
meter_and_prosody: A formal but flexible verse - rhyme and metre present but irregular - with a diction that moves between the journalistic ('a commercial photograph'), the historical ('bell-cheeked Negro infantry') and the visionary ('the blessèd break'); short lines and heavy stresses in the climactic stanzas; the last three lines are among the most famous in postwar American poetry.
historical_context: First read at the Boston Arts Festival in June 1960 and collected as the title poem of For the Union Dead (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1964); its occasion was the excavation of Boston Common for an underground garage and the demolition of the South Boston Aquarium in 1954, and its monument is Augustus Saint-Gaudens's bronze relief of Colonel Robert Gould Shaw and the 54th Massachusetts Volunteer Infantry, dedicated in 1897. The title echoes Allen Tate's 'Ode to the Confederate Dead', and the poem belongs to the civil-rights years in which Lowell marched in Washington and wrote against the war in Vietnam.
literary_significance: Lowell's best-known public poem and one of the central American poems of the 1960s; it is a standard text in the study of the poetry of history and of civil rights, it gave its name to one of the defining books of his career, and its closing image of 'a savage servility' is among the most quoted endings in modern American verse.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in For the Union Dead (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1964); first read at the Boston Arts Festival in 1960. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the relation between public memory and present indifference: the monument commemorates a sacrifice for racial justice, and the city that raised it is now building a garage beneath it and driving past it. Its second subject is the poet's own history, since the Aquarium and the Common belong to his Boston childhood and the monument to his family's ancestry on both sides of the Civil War; the sixth stanza's memory of the 'cowed' prisoners is the poem's acknowledgment that the poet's inheritance is compromised. The civil-rights images of the 1960s, which Lowell saw on television, belong to the poem's final movement and make it, with 'Skunk Hour' and the poems of Near the Ocean, one of the central American poems of the decade.
summary: Eight eight-line stanzas of loose rhymed verse in which the poet describes the excavation of the Common for an underground garage, the 'shaking' monument, the story of Shaw and his Black regiment, the loss of the Aquarium, a remembered childhood street, and the cars that 'nose forward like fish' at the end.
critical_context: Criticism has read the poem as an elegy for a lost civic ideal, as a meditation on the poet's own family history and on the monument as an object of art, and as a civil-rights poem of the early 1960s; the relation of the poem to Tate's 'Ode to the Confederate Dead' and to Saint-Gaudens's relief has been extensively discussed, and the epigraph's alteration of the Latin inscription is the standard example of Lowell's habit of revising public texts for his own purposes.
research_notes: The poem's first periodical publication was not identified; the 1964 date is the book date in the Norton list, and the 1960 first reading is documented. The Latin of the epigraph and the inscription on the monument differ, which the record states rather than resolves.

title: For Esmé—with Love and Squalor
description: A story published in The New Yorker on 8 April 1950 and collected in Nine Stories (1953): an American sergeant in Devon before D-Day meets a thirteen-year-old girl and her small brother, and a second episode in occupied Bavaria shows him recovering from a breakdown with her letter in his hands.
plot_or_argument: The story opens with a wedding invitation the narrator cannot accept and his decision to send 'a few written notes' about the bride, whom he met nearly six years before. The first episode is Devon in 1944, on a stormy afternoon during the last weeks of training for the invasion: the narrator, a sergeant, walks into town, listens to a children's choir rehearsal in a church, and is struck by the 'melodious and unsentimental' singing of one girl of about thirteen. He takes shelter in a tearoom and finds her there with her little brother Charles and their governess. Esmé - orphaned, her father killed in North Africa, her mother dead - wears her father's oversized military wristwatch and talks to the lonely American with a composure beyond her years, asking him to write to her and telling him that she wants to be a 'cold person' and is trying to be 'more compassionate'. The second episode moves to Bavaria after V-E Day and shifts to the third person: Sergeant X has returned from a field hospital after a nervous breakdown, cannot sleep, cannot read, and is visited by 'Corporal Z' (Clay), who lectures him on the lessons of the war - 'God, I love a good soldier' - and shows no feeling for what X has been through. After Clay leaves, X opens his unopened mail and finds a small package from Devon posted nearly a year before: Esmé's letter, written in her careful hand, and her father's wristwatch - 'a talisman' - which she asks him to wear for the duration of the war. The story ends there, with X's hands trembling, and the last line of the story is the only comment on it.
narrative_structure: A frame and two episodes: the invitation, the Devon afternoon and the Bavarian evening, with a deliberate shift from the first person to the third person and a change of the narrator's name to 'Sergeant X' between the episodes; the story withholds the union of the two until the parcel is opened, and its ending is a 'happy' ending that is also a diagnosis.
meter_and_prosody: A precise, artfully casual first-person style in the framing sections, with long sentences that shift between irony and tenderness; dialogue that catches Esmé's careful, slightly formal speech and Charles's chatter; the third-person episode in Bavaria written in a flatter, more withdrawn register; the letter reproduced at the end in Esmé's own idiom, which is the story's emotional climax.
historical_context: Published in The New Yorker on 8 April 1950, after being returned once and cut by six pages, and collected in Nine Stories (Little, Brown, 1953); Salinger had served in the 4th Infantry Division and landed on Utah Beach on D-Day, and the story was conceived as a tribute to veterans still suffering from what was then called battle fatigue. It is one of the earliest and most influential American treatments of combat trauma in fiction, and it belongs to the postwar American short story of the war, with the stories of Irwin Shaw and James Jones.
literary_significance: Salinger's most admired story and one of the finest American short stories of the century; it is the story through which his war experience is usually discussed, it is a standard anthology text and a frequent set text on the literature of trauma, and its two-part structure and its shift of narrative person are regularly taught as a model of the modern short story's technique.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The New Yorker, 8 April 1950; collected in Nine Stories (Boston: Little, Brown, 1953), published in the United Kingdom as For Esmé—with Love and Squalor and Other Stories. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story is about the damage war does to the capacity for feeling, and about the possibility of being brought back: Sergeant X's breakdown is described as a failure of the 'faculties' - he cannot sleep, read, feel or pray - and Esmé's gift works because it is disinterested, unsentimental and addressed to him as a person rather than as a soldier. The two episodes are also a study in the difference between 'love' and 'squalor': the title's terms are the story's argument, and the wedding-narrator's voice is the voice of a man who has recovered enough to be ironic. Salinger's decision to make the girl the moral centre, and to let her be neither saintly nor sentimental, is the story's most distinctive choice, and it belongs to his lifelong interest in the wisdom of children.
summary: Two episodes joined by a frame: the narrator's refusal of a wedding invitation and his written notes on the bride, then the rainy afternoon in Devon in 1944 with Esmé and Charles, and then the scene in Bavaria after V-E Day in which Sergeant X, shattered by the war, opens a parcel posted almost a year earlier.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story as Salinger's most successful treatment of the war, as a study in the ethics of the gift and of the letter, and as a story about the possibility of recovery; its shift from 'I' to 'Sergeant X' has been much discussed as a way of dramatising dissociation, and its portrait of Esmé has divided critics between those who see a sentimental idealisation of the child and those who see a carefully unsentimental portrait. It is regularly compared with 'A Perfect Day for Bananafish', its companion in Nine Stories.
research_notes: The story was not read complete; the summary follows the published text as described in the sources consulted, and the quotations are short and were checked against more than one transcription.

title: On the Road
description: Published by Viking on 5 September 1957: Sal Paradise's account of his journeys across America in 1947-50 with Dean Moriarty, a young ex-convict and car thief, in a book that made the road, the car and the jazz club the images of postwar American freedom.
plot_or_argument: Sal Paradise, a young writer living with his aunt in Paterson, New Jersey, has just finished a book and is recovering from a divorce when he meets Dean Moriarty, a wild, handsome, fast-talking young man from Denver who has spent time in reformatories and is newly married to a girl called Marylou. Part One follows Sal's first journey west in July 1947 - the buses and the hitch-hiking, the nights in Denver with Dean and their friend Carlo Marx, the ghost town of Central City, the job as a night watchman near San Francisco, the affair with Terry, a Mexican girl, and the cotton fields of California - and his return to New York. Part Two is the winter of 1948-49, when Dean arrives at Christmas with Marylou and the Dodge, and Sal, Dean and Marylou drive to New Orleans and on to San Francisco, where Dean abandons Sal for his wife Camille. Part Three is the spring of 1949: Sal in Denver, a trip to Mexico City, and Dean's arrival to take him to New York, where Sal meets the woman he calls 'the girl' and Dean leaves. Part Four is 1950, the great journey to Mexico with Dean, Sal and the poet Remi Boncoeur, and Part Five is the return to New York and Dean's last, brief appearance before he goes back west. The book's famous scenes - the drive to the Mexican border, the jazz clubs of San Francisco and New York, the 'mad ones' speech - are held together by Dean's energy and by Sal's growing awareness that the freedom he admires is also a form of irresponsibility.
narrative_structure: Five parts of very unequal length, each corresponding to a journey or a period in Sal's life; the narrative is episodic and picaresque, held together by the recurrence of Dean and by the first-person voice; the prose is spontaneous, paratactic and run on with dashes and colons, and the book's chronology is deliberately approximate.
meter_and_prosody: Kerouac's 'spontaneous bop prosody': long breathless sentences, strings of present participles, improvised lists of names and places, jazz-derived rhythms and repetitions; slang, profanity and Catholic devotional language side by side; a first-person narrator who is both inside and observing the action.
historical_context: Written in April 1951 on a continuous roll of taped-together paper in a three-week burst, then revised for years and heavily edited by Viking's editors before publication on 5 September 1957; the book's characters are portraits of Kerouac, Neal Cassady, Allen Ginsberg, William Burroughs and others, and its publication made Kerouac the spokesman of the Beat Generation and was received as a scandal and a manifesto at once.
literary_significance: The central novel of the Beat Generation and one of the defining American books of the 1950s; it named a youth culture, gave American prose a new speed and sound, has been continuously in print and widely taught since, and its manuscript roll is a canonical object of American literary history; it is the work through which the postwar counterculture and the road narrative are studied.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Viking Press (New York) on 5 September 1957; the original 1951 manuscript roll was published as On the Road: The Original Scroll (New York: Viking, 2007). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The novel's subject is the pursuit of 'it' - ecstasy, authenticity, the next party, the next saxophone solo - and its discovery that the pursuit destroys the people who follow it. Dean is both the novel's hero and its casualty: he leaves wives and children behind, steals cars and ends the book in rags, and Sal's love for him does not prevent the reader from seeing the damage. The road is the novel's image of American possibility and of American restlessness, and its landscape - the plains, the Denver mountains, the Mexican desert - is described with a lyricism that gives the book its lasting power. Behind the freedom is a melancholy, Catholic and Buddhist at once, that becomes explicit in Kerouac's later books.
summary: Five parts, three of them road trips with Dean, moving from Paterson, New Jersey, to Denver, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Mexico City, and filled with the people Sal and Dean meet on the way - hitch-hikers, waitresses, farm workers, musicians, junkies and friends.
critical_context: Criticism has read the novel as a picaresque, as a spiritual autobiography, as a document of postwar masculinity and of the Beats' marginalisation of women, and as a formal experiment in spontaneous prose. Its portraits of Cassady and Ginsberg and its treatment of race, class and sexuality have been much discussed, and the relation of the published text to the 1951 manuscript roll (published as On the Road: The Original Scroll in 2007) has become a subject of its own.
research_notes: The novel was not read complete; the summary follows the published text as described in the sources consulted, and quotations are limited to well-known phrases. The Norton selection is printed as an extract, and the record is the whole novel.

title: Harrison Bergeron
description: A story published in The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction in October 1961 and collected in Welcome to the Monkey House (1968): in 2081 the United States has made everyone equal by law, and a fourteen-year-old boy who refuses his handicaps is shot dead on live television.
plot_or_argument: The story opens with the sentence that has become its signature: 'The year was 2081, and everybody was finally equal.' The equality is enforced by constitutional amendment and by the Handicapper General, Diana Moon Glampers, whose agents fit the strong with weights, the beautiful with masks and the intelligent with radios that broadcast noises into their ears every twenty seconds. George Bergeron, who is intelligent and strong, wears a forty-seven-pound bag of birdshot around his neck and a radio in his ear; his wife Hazel is of perfectly average intelligence and needs no handicap. They are watching a ballet on television - the ballerinas are masked and weighted - when a bulletin announces that their son Harrison, fourteen years old, seven feet tall and burdened with three hundred pounds of handicaps, has escaped from prison. Harrison storms the studio, tears off his handicaps and the ballerina's, declares himself emperor, chooses the ballerina as his empress and dances with her to the musicians' 'best' music. Diana Moon Glampers enters with a double-barrelled shotgun and kills them both; the television goes dark. George, who has left the room to get a beer, returns and asks Hazel why she has been crying; she says something sad happened on television but she cannot remember what it was.
narrative_structure: A single continuous scene of a few pages, with no chapters or breaks, in which the television broadcast, the parents' conversation and Harrison's irruption are intercut; the story's time is compressed into an evening and its exposition is delivered through the broadcast and the narrator's flat commentary.
meter_and_prosody: Short declarative sentences and very short paragraphs; a deadpan, faux-naive narrator who reports atrocity as ordinary fact; repeated phrases ('everybody was finally equal', 'that was the law') used as a refrain; dialogue in the flat idiom of television and bureaucracy; almost no metaphor, so that the few images (the birdshot bag, the shotgun) carry great weight.
historical_context: Published in The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction in October 1961 and collected in Welcome to the Monkey House (Delacorte, 1968); it belongs to Vonnegut's early period of magazine science fiction, written while he was working for General Electric and publishing in the slicks and the pulps, and it was adapted for television and film several times, most notably in the 1995 Showtime film.
literary_significance: One of the most widely anthologised American short stories of the century and a standard school text on dystopia, equality and the state; its opening sentence is one of the best known in American fiction, and the story is a frequent point of reference in political argument about merit and levelling, which has made it both unusually influential and unusually contested.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction, October 1961; collected in Welcome to the Monkey House (New York: Delacorte Press, 1968). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story is a reductio ad absurdum of one reading of equality: a society that levels down every excellence to the lowest common denominator produces not justice but a numb, supervised mediocrity in which no one can think, feel or remember. Its satire is aimed at bureaucratic egalitarianism, and the story is regularly taught - and regularly contested - as an argument about equality and excellence; Vonnegut's own politics were egalitarian, and the story's target is more precisely the deadening of individuality by the state than equality as such. The ending, in which Hazel cannot remember her son's death, is the story's real horror: the handicaps have done their work on memory itself.
summary: A short story of some twelve hundred words set in 2081, in which George and Hazel Bergeron watch a television ballet, their son Harrison escapes from prison, seizes a studio and is killed by the Handicapper General, and his parents cannot remember what they have seen.
critical_context: The story has been read as a satire of enforced egalitarianism, as a Cold War parable about conformity and as a metafictional joke about the reader's own desire for a level playing field; critics have debated whether its target is equality itself (a reading Vonnegut resisted) or the bureaucratic administration of equality, and its portrait of Hazel and of the ballerinas has been central to feminist and disability readings of the story.
research_notes: Read through the text reproduced in anthologies and in the sources consulted; the quotations are short and were checked against more than one transcription.

title: Slaughterhouse-Five
description: Published by Delacorte on 31 March 1969, subtitled 'The Children's Crusade: A Duty-Dance with Death': the life of Billy Pilgrim, a prisoner of war in Dresden during the firebombing of 1945, who becomes 'unstuck in time' and is exhibited in a zoo on another planet, told in fragments by a narrator who is also a character.
plot_or_argument: The novel opens with a chapter in which 'I' - a narrator closely identified with Vonnegut - describes returning to Dresden in 1967 with his old war friend Bernard O'Hare, trying and failing for years to write a book about the firebombing, and beginning the book with the Children's Crusade and the famous first line 'All this happened, more or less.' The second chapter introduces Billy Pilgrim, an optometrist from Ilium, New York, who has come unstuck in time: he travels without warning between moments of his life, and the novel follows him through them. As a chaplain's assistant in 1944 he is captured in Luxembourg, survives the cattle cars, arrives in Dresden as a prisoner of war, and is working in a malt-syrup factory when the city is destroyed in February 1945; with the other prisoners he is put to work clearing the bodies. Later, abducted by the Tralfamadorians, he is kept in a zoo with the film star Montana Wildhack and learns their philosophy - that all moments exist simultaneously, that the dead are always alive in their own moments, and that the appropriate response to death is 'So it goes'. In the present of the novel's 1960s, Billy survives a plane crash, is nursed by his daughter, goes on television to tell the world about Tralfamadore, and is murdered in 1976 by Paul Lazzaro. The novel ends with the prisoners in Dresden and with the birdsong that follows the bombing, and with the narrator's acknowledgement that the book he has written is a failure and his son's war in Vietnam is not over.
narrative_structure: Ten chapters moving non-chronologically through Billy's life, with the narrator's own voice intruding in the first and last chapters and briefly in between; the Tralfamadorian episodes, the war, the optometrist's family life and the Dresden material are interleaved in short sections, so that the reader experiences time as Billy does. The book's fragments are held together by repeated phrases, by the refrain 'So it goes' and by the recurring image of the blue and ivory feet of the dead and dying.
meter_and_prosody: Short, flat sentences and very short paragraphs; deadpan irony and a naively precise notation of detail; refrain and repetition used as structure; lists, songs and doggerel poems embedded in the text; a tone that moves from slapstick to sorrow within a paragraph, and a narrator whose sentimentality is offered without embarrassment.
historical_context: Published by Delacorte Press on 31 March 1969 and dedicated to Mary O'Hare and Bernard V. O'Hare; Vonnegut had been a prisoner of war in Dresden and had worked for years on a book about it, visiting the city in 1967 with O'Hare. The novel appeared during the Vietnam War, was burned in a school board furnace in Drake, North Dakota, in 1973, and became one of the defining anti-war books of the American 1960s and 1970s; it was filmed by George Roy Hill in 1972.
literary_significance: Vonnegut's masterpiece and one of the central American novels of the postwar period; it is a standard text on the literature of war and of trauma, on postmodern narrative and on the 1960s, it has never been out of print, and its first chapter is often taught as an essay on the ethics of writing history.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Delacorte Press (New York) on 31 March 1969. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The novel's central subject is the firebombing of Dresden and the impossibility of writing about it: the first chapter is an essay on that impossibility, and the rest of the book answers it with a form that refuses chronology, causation and moral summary. Tralfamadorian time is the novel's device for expressing trauma - if all moments exist at once, then nothing is lost and nothing can be changed, and 'So it goes' is both consolation and evasion. The novel is also about the American war in Vietnam, about the slaughter of civilians in the name of the state, and about the 'children's crusade' that sends adolescents to die; its deadpan treatment of death has been read as a way of holding grief at arm's length and as a way of insisting on continuing to feel it.
summary: Ten chapters and a first chapter about the writing of the book, moving without transition between Billy's childhood, his war, his optometry practice in Ilium, New York, his abduction by the Tralfamadorians, the death of his wife, the death of his son in Vietnam and the Dresden firestorm, with the phrase 'So it goes' following every death.
critical_context: Criticism reads the novel as a postmodern war narrative, as a trauma narrative whose form imitates dissociation, and as a satire of American optimism and of the conventions of science fiction; the function of Tralfamadore, the meaning of 'So it goes' and the relation of the narrator to Vonnegut are the central debates. Its censorship history, from the Drake school board to later challenges, is a standard case study in American book banning.
research_notes: The novel was not read complete; the summary follows the published text as described in the sources consulted, and quotations are limited to the best-known phrases. The Norton selection is printed as an extract, and the record is the whole novel.

title: A Conversation with My Father
description: A story published in New American Review in 1972 and collected in Enormous Changes at the Last Minute (1974): a writer visits her dying father, who asks her to write a simple story, and the two versions she produces - one tragic, one open - become an argument about how fiction should end.
plot_or_argument: The story begins with the father's request: 'I would like you to write a simple story just once more, the kind you used to write when you were a little girl.' He is old, ill with heart disease, and knows that he is dying; he lies in bed in his apartment with the curtains drawn, and his daughter, a writer in middle age, comes to sit with him and agrees. She invents a neighbour, a woman with a son who becomes a drug addict, and tells the story with the ending the father wants - the son dies, the woman is destroyed, everything is tragic and complete. The father is pleased. But the narrator is not satisfied, and she tells the story again: this time the son survives, the mother learns to live with him, and the story ends not with a death but with a possibility. The father rejects the second version as 'not a story' - it does not end, it does not conclude, it does not tell the truth about life. Their conversation moves between the two versions and between their two ideas of what a story is for: the father holds that a story must acknowledge tragedy, face death and end, while the daughter holds that a story may leave its people alive and its ending open, and that a life is not improved by being made into a conclusion. The father's illness is present throughout, since the story's occasion is the fact that he is dying, and the argument about fiction is also an argument about how to face that. The story ends with the father's reproach and the daughter's unresolved reply.
narrative_structure: A frame conversation with two embedded narratives: the father's request, the first version of the story, the father's approval, the second version, and the father's rejection, with the narrator's commentary between them; the story's movement is dialectical rather than plot-driven, and it ends in disagreement rather than resolution.
meter_and_prosody: A talky, conversational first-person voice with short paragraphs and abrupt transitions; dialogue in which the father's old-world idiom and the daughter's modern one are sharply distinguished; direct address and repetition; the embedded stories told in a plainer style than the frame, so that the difference between them is audible.
historical_context: Published in New American Review in 1972 and collected in Enormous Changes at the Last Minute (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1974); the father is Paley's own father, Isaac Goodside, a doctor, and the story belongs to the feminist experimental fiction of the early 1970s and to the tradition of metafictional stories about storytelling that runs from Sterne through Borges to Barth.
literary_significance: Paley's most discussed story and one of the central American short stories of the 1970s; it is a standard text in courses on metafiction, on the short story and on American women's writing, and it is one of the clearest statements in postwar American fiction of the argument that narrative form is a political and ethical choice.
bibliographical_notes: First published in New American Review in 1972; collected in Enormous Changes at the Last Minute (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1974) and in The Collected Stories (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1994). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story is about the difference between two kinds of truth: the father's, which demands that art acknowledge tragedy and conclude, and the daughter's, which refuses to close experience off and insists that a story may leave its people alive. Around that argument gathers the story's other subjects - the relation of a daughter to a dying father, the ethics of using real people in fiction (the narrator's story is invented, but the conversation is not), and the feminist critique of narrative form, since the closed, tragic ending is associated with the father and the open one with the daughter. Paley's preface to Enormous Changes - 'Everyone in this book is imagined into life except the father. No matter what story he has to live in, he's my father' - is the story's own frame.
summary: A short story in two movements, in which the unnamed daughter sits by her bedridden father's side and tells him the story of a woman and her drug-addicted son, twice: first as a conventional tragedy that the father approves of, and then as a story that refuses to end in tragedy, which the father rejects.
critical_context: Criticism has read the story as metafiction, as a feminist critique of closure, as a study in mourning and as Paley's ars poetica; the two versions of the story-within-the-story are regularly analysed as models of the tragic and the open ending, and the father's demand for a simple story has been discussed in relation to the immigrant parent's relation to American realism.
research_notes: The story was not read complete; the summary follows the published text as described in the sources consulted, and the quotations are the best-known lines.

title: Zagrowsky Tells
description: A story published in Mother Jones in May 1985 and collected in Later the Same Day the same year: an elderly Jewish pharmacist in the Bronx, talking to the narrator on a park bench, defends himself against the charge of racism by telling the story of his daughter, his grandson and the Black woman who bore him.
plot_or_argument: The story is spoken almost entirely by Mr. Zagrowsky, a retired pharmacist who runs into the narrator, Faith, in a park and begins to talk. He is aggrieved: he has been accused of racism by the Black and Puerto Rican customers of his pharmacy, and he wants to explain himself. His explanation is a family history - his daughter Eileen, who had a breakdown and spent years in and out of hospitals; the child she had with a Black man, who was left to her parents to raise; his wife's refusal to accept the child; and his own slow, unwilling, and finally absolute love for the boy, whom he calls his grandson and whose name he says with pride. The story's action is entirely in the telling: Zagrowsky reveals, without ever admitting it, that his own life has been changed by exactly the people he thinks he is defending himself against, and the narrator's few interjections show that she is hearing something other than what he means to say. The story ends with him still talking, unrepentant and, in spite of himself, moving.
narrative_structure: A dramatic monologue with a thin frame: Zagrowsky speaks for almost the whole story, and the narrator's presence is registered in brief questions, reported gestures and occasional corrections; the story has no plot in the conventional sense, only the gradual unfolding of a family history through the speaker's resistance to it.
meter_and_prosody: Paley's reproduced Bronx speech: run-on sentences, repetitions, self-interruptions, insults, direct address ('You know what I'm saying?'), and sudden turns into tenderness; the narrator's voice is much quieter, so that the contrast between the two is part of the story's meaning.
historical_context: Published in Mother Jones in May 1985 and collected in Later the Same Day (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1985); Zagrowsky had appeared in Paley's earlier story 'The Used-Boy Raisers' and Faith Darwin is the semi-autobiographical character who recurs across her collections; the story belongs to the New York Jewish fiction of the 1980s and to the feminist short story of the same years.
literary_significance: One of Paley's most admired late stories and a standard example of the American dramatic monologue in fiction; it is the story through which her late style and her treatment of race and ethnicity are usually discussed, and its method - letting a bigoted speaker reveal his own transformation - is frequently taught as a model of indirect characterisation.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Mother Jones, May 1985; collected in Later the Same Day (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1985) and in The Collected Stories (1994). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story is about the gap between a man's opinions and his life: Zagrowsky's talk is full of racial insult and self-pity, and his actions - taking in his mixed-race grandson, raising him, loving him - contradict everything he says. Paley's method is to let him condemn himself out of his own mouth and then to let the reader see what he cannot see: that he has already been changed. The story is also about the ethics of the storyteller, since the narrator is a writer listening for material, and about the Bronx as a place where ethnic and racial groups live close together and talk past one another.
summary: A single monologue - Zagrowsky's account, punctuated by the narrator's brief questions and corrections - in which the pharmacist remembers his daughter's breakdown, the child she had with a Black man, the family's refusal of the child, and his own late, grudging love for his grandson.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story as a study in the ethics of letting a character speak, and as one of the few American stories of its period to treat a white ethnic character's racism through his own family history; the relation between Zagrowsky's speech and his actions is the central topic, and the story is often compared with Paley's earlier 'The Used-Boy Raisers' and with the Faith Darwin stories around it.
research_notes: The story was not read complete; the summary follows the published text as described in the sources consulted, and the quotations are limited to characteristic phrases rather than exact lines.
